member of the Renfrew county council. He has as well been a member of the Ontario legislature and, as in the case of the hon. member for Lotbiniere, his address this afternoon afforded evidence of the experience which he has already attained in public life. His address has made apparent that we have had added to our number one who is particularly interested in the well-being of the farming community; one who has a broad interest in questions of the day and an hon. member who is well able to participate effectively in the discussions of the house.
I should like, in addition to welcoming these two new members to the house, to extend a welcome also to the other members who have entered parliament for the first time at this session: the hon. member for Cape Breton North-Victoria (Mr. MacLean); the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. McCallum), and the hon. member for St. Henry (Mr. Bonnier). We shall have with us in a few days, I hope, the hon. member for Victoria, (B.C.) (Mr. Mayhew), who, unfortunately, is indisposed at the present time. All these gentlemen, will, I trust, have useful careers in this parliament in the service of their country.
There is one other hon. gentleman who I am also glad to see again in his seat in this house, our friend the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). With his usual modesty he did not permit himself to be reintroduced to the house. May I say to him that we are glad to see him back again in the fold, as I am sure he is glad to be back. I have no doubt that, after his little escapade last summer and autumn in provincial politics, he has come back a much wiser though perhaps a somewhat sadder man.
Now may I say to my right hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) that we all enjoyed very much some of the humour of his speech. We have been entertained by his digressions in many directions, although it has been a little difficult to follow him in some of his denunciations, exclamations, innuendoes and insinuations. I am not going to try to follow him along that devious course. I was however somewhat surprised that he was not a little more courteous to one of the hon. members who has just come into this house, who he had heard speaking for only a very few minutes and who he would not permit even to ask a question when, in the mind of the hon. member for Renfrew North, the right hon. gentleman himself was misconstruing what that hon. member had just been saying.
My right hon. friend said that the hon. member for Renfrew North had been drawing on his imagination for the facts. Well, there

are some things with respect to which we need not draw on our imagination to be perfectly sure of the facts. One is that the present administration received from the people of this country the largest majority that any administration has had in the history of Canada. Nor do we need to draw on our imagination to recall that while for a time my right hon. friend was the leader of a very large party, he got at the end of one term of office one of the worst defeats any prime minister ever received. Nor do we need to draw on our imagination for a further fact, one which I think is also important, in view of what my right hon. friend has had to say [by way of erititcism of the government, particularly with reference to what he says we have failed to do, in the matter of improving conditions. Let me ask: How has the country itself viewed the actions of the government since it took office? We have had seventeen by-elections since the general elections of 1935. Of that number my right hon. friend has carried three and the present administration fourteen. Of the three which my right hon. friend and his party have carried, one was in the city of Victoria. Since that by-election, there has been a second in this same constituency and the seat has been lost by my right hon. friend's party. One of the other two was the by-election which returned my hon. friend from Dufferin-Simcoe, of whom I spoke a moment ago. Evidently he was quite overcome by the few kindly remarks which were made about him, for he has left the chamber. The hon. member was allowed to leave this house by one of its doors and to come back unopposed by the same door.
There is still another fact to be kept in mind, it is not something imagined. While the present government was returned to power after the general elections of 1935 with the largest majority any administration has ever had in the history of Canada, to-day, at the beginning of the third session of the present parliament, we enjoy an even larger majority than we had at the time we came into office.
It is the country's opinion, I value. So, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to devote too much time .to what my right hon. friend has said about our failure to help meet the situation as it exists in this country. He has said a great deal about unemployment, which he states is continuing. May I remind the house of what my right hon. friend told the electorate when he was appealing to them and when they returned him to office in 1930? He promised that he would end unemployment or perish in the attempt. Far from perishing, he is here in livelier form than ever.

My right hon. friend talks about the number of unemployed, but the numbers of unemployed to-day are very different from what they were during his period of office, fortunately for the people and for the incomes of the people, to which his amendment to-night relates.
I was pleased, as we all were, to hear the reference the right hon. gentleman made to Their Majesties the King and Queen. Those of us who were privileged to attend the coronation ceremonies were deeply impressed by what we witnessed in Westminster Abbey. Even more impressive, however, than the consecration by their majesties of their lives at that service, is the devotion which they have shown to the public service in their high post of duty since his majesty's accession. I doubt if at any time in the history of any country there have been upon the throne a king and queen more devoted to each other and to their subjects, and whose lives have been more completely consecrated to the wellbeing of their fellow men, than King George VI and Queen Elizabeth. The affection in which they are held in the old land is already all but equalled by the affection entertained for them in all parts of their great empire.
The speech from the throne affords, I think, an appropriate opportunity for a reference to the recognition given in the coronation cere-money to the complete nationhood of the Dominion of Canada. I confess that as I listened to the oath which was administered to his majesty, and heard his majesty promise to obey it, I felt great pride as a Canadian to hear for the first time in history my own country in relation to the crown mentioned in terms exactly the same as those applied to Great Britain itself. The oath administered at the time of the coronation ceremony was as follows:
Will you solemnly promise and swear to govern the peoples of Great Britain, Ireland, Canada, Australia, New' Zealand and the Union of South Africa, of your possessions and the other territories to any of them belonging or pertaining, and of your empire of India, according to their respective laws and customs?
The reply was:
I solemnly promise so to do.
That oath marks the end of a suggestion, remote or otherwise, of anything in the nature of subordinate or colonial status. It is the enunciation by the crown itself of the complete nationhood of Canada on equality, so far as status is concerned, with all other nations of the British Commonwealth.
I found it somewhat difficult to follow the observations of my right hon. friend with regard to the imperial conference. So far as I

am able to recollect, his observations were to the effect that speeches were reported to have been made by me, or that something had appeared somewhere referring to me, purporting that, at the imperial conference, I had acted as the chief interpreter' of the views of the chief executive of another country with respect to that country's relationship with Great Britain.
Why did my right hon. friend not come right out and state that some Conservative papens, here and there, have been saying that Mr. Mackenzie King was seeking to be of some service to the President of the United States in connection with his desire to conclude ,a trade agreement with Great Britain. That is what he meant, but he did not say it. He left it as a sort of vague impression, one which has been fostered right and left in the press supporting my right hon. friend. In fact, in an editorial in one of the papers of this city there appeared the statement that, when last year I visited Washington as the guest of the president, the purpose of my visit was to discuss the proposed trade agreement with Great Britain, that I had gone very fully into the whole matter with the president and with the secretary of state, and that I had then gone to the imperial conference and at the conference had been the advocate for the United States with respect to an agreement with Great Britain.
May I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to hon. members, that at the time I visited Mr. Roosevelt at the White House in the early part of last year, and had the privilege of discussing a great many questions with him in an intimate way, the subject of a trade agreement between the United States and Great Britain was never so much as mentioned. The same is literally and absolutely true with respect to any conversation I had with the Secretary of State for the United States at that time, or with any member of the United States government.
It was from the British Ambassador in Washington, and from our own minister in Washington who, in turn, had received his information from the British Ambassador, that I learned for the first time that for some little time there had been explorations, negotiations, conversations, whatever the proper description may be, with respect to the possibility of a trade agreement between the United States and Great Britain. It was information given, not with any request attached to it, but a simple statement of the fact that these two countries were contemplating negotiations and had begun discussions.

When, with some of my colleagues, I was present at one of the sessions of the Imperial conference in London, the matter was brought up, not at my instance, as was stated from some inspired source, but by a minister of the crown in Great Britain. The question was discussed openly before the representatives of the empire countries there represented, in which number Canada was included. We were told of the nature of the negotiations under way and were asked to express our views with regard to them. I need not say to this House of Commons that any expression of views from any of my colleagues or myself was wholly to the effect that, while Canada was anxious in every way to be of service in the matter of furthering friendly relationships among different countries, we would necessarily wish to see that every privilege we enjoyed in the British market was fully protected, and that any change which might be made in that position could be made only as the result of what in our opinion were adequate compensations therefor.
I do not propose to-night to go into the matter of trade negotiations between Great Britain and the United States, or for that matter into trade negotiations between Canada and the United States. I shall have something to say on these matters at a later date. Part of the business of a leader of an opposition is, so far as possible, to draw out the government in advance of the time at which discussions on certain subjects may properly take place. The time to discuss these trade matters is when we have something concrete before us for deliberation.
I should, however, make it abundantly clear that any trade negotiations between Great Britain and the United States were begun and entered into by those countries themselves. Of necessity we have to take notice of them. We have an agreement with Great Britain and one with the United States, each of which will expire shortly. In fact, the one with the United States runs to the end of the present year, and is subject thereafter upon notice to complete cancellation at the end of six months. The agreement with Great Britain expires in 1940.
It is necessary for a government at all times to have regard, not only for today but for to-morrow, to have regard to situations which may arise not in the immediate present only but also in the future. Under these circumstances I would ask any hon. member this question: When other countries belonging to the British Commonwealth of Nations have declared their willingness to cooperate helpfully, if it is possible so to do, in the further-

ance of trade relations between the two greatest trading countries of the world, in a manner which it is hoped will help to serve the interests not only of these two countries but of all parts of the British Commonwealth and other nations as well, should Canada be the one to sit back, like a dog in the manger and say, "We will have nothing to do with either of you in transactions of the kind "? I wonder where we would be in the course of another year if that were the attitude we chose to take.
If that is the attitude he would take, it is a fortunate thing for Canada that my right hon. friend is not in office to-day. I tell him that, strongly as he may feel about the importance of having a wall around this country, the walls which have been built up around different countries are more than anything else, responsible for the unrest throughout the world at the present time. The world will get through its present difficulties, not by nations adopting an attitude of non-cooperation, but by all countries being as helpful as they can and in as many directions as possible. Particularly is this true with respect to matters tending to improve conditions in international trade.
The next topic to which reference is made in the speech from the throne is the improvement in Canada's economic condition. The facts of recovery are so evident, I had thought I would not say very much on this subject, but the amendment of my right hon. friend forces me to make some observations. He has moved the following in amendment:
We desire respectfully to express regret that the, speech from the throne does not indicate that the government have taken or contemplate taking efficient measures to deal with unfavourable economic conditions in Canada, and that no legislative action is proposed to deal effectively with the prevailing uncertainty and insecurity resulting from the inadequate incomes of large numbers of our people.
The amendment regrets that the speech from the throne does not indicate that the government have taken or contemplate taking efficient measures to improve economic conditions. Why should the speech from the throne state that the government contemplates taking efficient measures to improve economic conditions? Look at the facts and figures with regard to the present conditions in Canada in comparison with what they were when we came into office and see what they disclose. They speak more eloquently than any words in the speech from the throne could. If we inserted in the speech from the throne the exact words calculated to avoid my right bon. friend's amendment he would have criticized us at once. He would have

told :us that instead of putting any such words into the speech from the throne it would have been much better to have enumerated the statistics which would verify the fact that an improvement had taken place.
He said that within the last little while there had been a falling off of trade with the United States, that there had been a setback to some extent, and that the balance of trade was not what it had been. My right hon. friend knows very well that the falling off this year in exports to the United States and other countries is due, more than anything else to the unfortunate drought which has been experienced in western Canada. In the past year, the United States had a surplus of grains, feed and fodder, whereas Canada unfortunately, as a result of intense drought had no exportable surplus. A year ago that situation was entirely the reverse. At that time we had a surplus of these commodities and drought in the United States necessitated large imports of them from Canada. Because of drought, Canada did not have a normal quantity of wheat for export in the closing months of 1937. The exports of wheat in December, 1936, were valued at $25,256,000, whereas in December, 1937, they were valued at only $10,121,000. In the one item of wheat there was a decrease of $15,000,000 or 60 per cent in one month. This decrease was due in part, to the fact that the dominion had not been able to produce the wheat required for export. We hope that this condition will not recur in the present year, and there is strong reason to believe that it will not. If conditions should again become what we hope they will, then unquestionably sales to the United States and other countries will be appreciably increased as a consequence.

The coronation and the imperial conference made exceptional demands on the high commissioner's office. I wonder if hon. members realize how great that additional obligation w'as. There were arrangements for invitations to and the placing of Canadians in the abbey; the allocation of 4,800 tickets for Canadians to view the possession on the line of march, as well as the financing and administration of the sale of those tickets. At any rate the matter was very carefully considered by my colleagues and myself. On August 14 I replied to a communication which had come formally from Mr. Norris, president of Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated, asking if the application could not be granted. The letter dated Prime Minister's office, Canada. August 14, is as follows:

Dear Mr. Norris:
I wish to acknowledge your letter of August the 10th, just received, with reference to the application of the Cedars Rapids Manufacturing and Power Company, a subsidiary of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company, for a licence to export 40,000 horsepower to the United States for sole use by the Aluminum Company of America at Massena, New York.
The representations in your letter have received the most careful consideration of my colleagues and myself. I regret, however, that the government is not in a position to grant the licence, at the present time. In view of the broad question of policy involved and the fact that the export of power to the United States has been debated at length in parliament on several occasions, the government is of opinion that an opportunity should be afforded at the approaching session for a discussion on the subject, before any final action is taken with respect to the application of the Cedars Rapids Manufacturing and Power Company.
Yours sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King.

Early in
November I was waited on in my office by Mr. Powell, president of Aluminum Limited, of Montreal, in company with Mr. Geoffrion, his counsel. They asked if it would not be possible for the government to grant a licence to Aluminum Limited for the export of power. It was practically the same application as the one to which I have already referred. A few days later, a reply was sent to Mr. Powell on my behalf by Mr. Read, the acting Under-Secretary of State in language almost identical with that which I have just read. Mr. Powell and Mr. Geoffrion interviewed me on November 2. Mr. Read's reply was sent on November 12. On November 29 the Hon. Mr. Hepburn waited on myself and members of the government to ascertain whether the Dominion government would grant a licence to the Ontario Hydro Commission for the export of power. All I wish to draw attention to is this, that the government had in August, and again in November indicated in writing its position with respect to the granting of licences. On both occasions it had stated that no licence for the export of power would be given by the administration until after the matter had been fully discussed in this

parliament and the question of policy further and fully considered here. When the premier of Ontario met with my colleagues and myself, and preferred his request, we read him the communication that I have just read to the house, outlined the nature of previous discussions on the subject - < the export of power in this parliament, and indicated that, while we were prepared to consider the additional information that he had just then put at our disposal, we could not at that time consider granting the application in view of the government's position as previously adopted with respect to the two earlier applications, and as set forth in the communications to Mr. Norris and Mr. Powell.

I shall speak
on this question later and at that time give full particulars. What I wish to make perfectly clear to-night is this, that the government had determined and laid down its policy before it had any knowledge whatever that the Ontario government was contemplating applying for a licence, or of the negotiation of a settlement of its differences with some of the power companies. We made and could make no alteration in that policy when the premier of Ontario called upon us. When I told the premier that it was impossible for us to meet his wishes and gave him the reasons which I have given to the house to-night, naturally he was disappointed. My words to him were simply that, as an executive, we were the servants of parliament, not its masters. That is the position which this government is going to continue to take with respect to the export of electrical power from this country. It may be that there are circumstances and conditions which will justify one view or another with respect to what is most advisable as to the export of power. That may be discussed very fully and freely in this house. The words, however, injected by my right hon. friend into this debate which would seek to link in any way the present administration and its attitude towards the export of power with any matter which pertains to the franchise, are wholly uncalled for and wholly unworthy on his part.
The hour is late, but I wish to avoid if possible speaking in this debate again tomorrow. If the house will grant me a few minutes, I shall briefly conclude what I have to say.

My right hon. friend has spoken about the international situation. I agree with him whole-heartedly when he deplores much that has taken place in China, the way in which women and children have been treated in that country, and many other of the incidents which have marked the conflict there. I should not confine these feelings to what is happening in China. I also agree wholeheartedly with him that we cannot be too careful at this time of all times, to refrain from doing anything or saying anything which in any way can cause our neutrality to be suspected. These are dangerous times in the affairs of the world. My own feeling is that much of the unrest in our own country, many of those things that we describe as affecting the unity of Canada, are the result of a contagion of ill-will which has spread itself over the globe-inevitably, because ill-will is contagious just as good-will is contagious, and the one can only be offset by the other. It behooves us in this country of ours, blessed as we are in our geographical position, blessed as we are in our neighbours, blessed as we are in being part of the great British commonwealth of nations, to be very careful and very guarded in everything we do and say at this time.
If in some particulars it may seem to hon. members that the government is not going as far as it might go, is not doing some of the things which it might do and which many of us in our hearts would wish to do if we had the power necessary to back up our acts against all possible consequences, let them remember that there are other powers in this world as well as Canada which have great concern in the world situation, that other powers are deeply interested in all that happens in China as well as in Europe, and that if great powers like the United Kingdom, France and the United States think it wisest in the present world situation to refrain from taking some steps which might be construed in a different way than they would wish to have them construed, perhaps we ourselves are not acting unwisely, either in their interests or our own, in being equally cautious. Any one who has followed the attitude of the British government and some other governments towards .the situation in Spain must have been impressed with the fact, that time and time and time again these governments have refrained from asserting themselves in an extreme way, lest their action might provoke a still graver situation. They have remained seemingly silent under grave provocation. There are times when it takes much more in the way of courage to remain silent

in the face of seeming or actual insult and injustice than it does to be outspoken and to strike out from the shoulder. These are times when all the restraint that can be exercised by a country, a government or by members of parliament should be exercised. I do hope that, in the course of political discussions in this house during the present session, hon. members will think twice with regard to whatever they may have to say on foreign affairs, and ask themselves whether, in view of the attitude which great nations such as England, France and the United States have thought it wisest to adopt, we ourselves should seek to outrun them and attempt some of the things that go much farther than they are prepared to go.
With respect to the remarks attributed to the Hon. Mr. Bruce, may I say at once that no one regrets more than Mr. Bruce himself does that there should have been by him even so much as a mention of the situation in the orient. He so expressed himself to me, and in reference to the article referred to by my right hon. friend gave a statement to the press which I think ought to be put on record:
I would not be so indiscreet as to make a statement of that kind. The statement is entirely misleading. It is a misinterpretation of my remarks, although I do not consider that it was done with any deliberate intent.
I talked over the situation with Mr. Bruce, and I believe that, in so far as he may have spoken at all in private conversation with people in different parts of the country or with others, what at most he did was to indicate in some cases what he believed was in the mind of Japan; not that he was giving his view of the situation but that he was seeking to interpret, to those who could not comprehend the situation, what from the Japanese point of view the situation was considered to be. That, I would say myself, might just as well have been left unsaid. I agree with the criticism which the leader of the opposition has made to-night as regards a member of the diplomatic service having said anything at this time with respect to a situation so critical as that between China and Japan. But I do not think that we need enlarge upon it to any extent. I do not believe that the Chinese government or the Japanese government could for a moment think that this country was seeking to take sides in the unfortunate differences which have arisen and the conflict which is in progress. I believe they understand that our decision is to be strictly neutral, to hold ourselves in a position where, if opportunity does

offer, and some word of ours can help to shorten the conflict, to minimize the struggle, that word will be given in season and may prove of value.
Mr. Bruce has intimated to me that after the coming summer he would like to be relieved of his position as minister to Japan. When he accepted the position he did so with the understanding that it would be only for a year or two. He took the post to oblige the government. Sir Herbert Marler was being appointed to Washington and it was difficult to find anyone wholly qualified to take his place in Tokyo. Mr. Bruce has an understanding of conditions on the Pacific coast which very few men possess. He has a wide knowledge of affairs. Above all he has a disposition and a nature which can be relied upon not to antagonize those with whom he is brought into contact but to further cooperative effort.
Mr. Bruce has done exceedingly well in Tokyo. Reports from those who have met him, reports from our own people who have been in Japan while he has been there, make clear to me that his service to Canadians in or passing through Japan has been a very real one, and certainly the reports we receive from him have been extremely helpful to the government. It is true that his sight is greatly impaired; but there have been men whose sight has been impaired, but whose judgment has been all the keener, perhaps as a consequence. Mr. Bruce is of that type. He is accustomed to bring about him into conference each day those who are close to him in the legation, and through other eyes and the confidences imparted to him, he obtains, I believe, pretty much all that can be comprehended at the present time by any minister in regard to the situation in the orient.

Well, if this greater freedom of trade is a bad thing, why did his government try to do anything? I think my right hon. friend has let the cat out of the bag to-night. I do not believe he ever meant to put through an agreement with the United States, simply because he believes in economic nationalism and economic imperialism. Had he remained in office, that agreement would not exist to-day.
Does my right hon. friend recall what he said just before he came into office in 1930? Does he recall what he said as to how he would get into other markets? He was not going to take the slow way of seeking entry by agreement into foreign markets. He was going to blast his way into the markets of the world. And now he comes and tells us that this business of blasting one's way into world markets is all wrong. What we need, he now says, is not to get into the markets of the world; we need as a country, to be in a watertight compartment where we can work out our experiments; experiments to be worked out between the Conservative party and its new allies the Social Credit party in the west.
